items.headline: San Francisco starts same-day long-acting buprenorphine injections at a low-barrier clinic
items.summary: San Francisco's health department launched a pilot at the Maria X Martinez Health Resource Center that lets patients get a first dose of long-acting injectable buprenorphine on site, which the clinic could not store or give before. The roughly $500,000 pilot buys 460 starting doses and 500 follow-up doses over two years, runs through April 2028, and may expand to up to five more city clinics in 2027. The city will track overdoses, emergency use and retention, so clinicians should watch for outcome data on same-day injection starts.

items.headline: Mass General Brigham plans one ED opioid treatment model across its hospitals, starting with Salem
items.summary: Mass General Brigham says it is working to bring the model used at Massachusetts General and the Brigham to its other emergency departments: clinicians start buprenorphine in the ED, addiction specialists consult at the bedside, and walk-in bridge clinics continue care. Salem Hospital clinicians are beginning training, and a federal grant will fund a consult team and bridge clinic at Cooley Dickinson Hospital. This is the system's own account with no outcome data or timeline, but it shows a large system treating ED opioid treatment starts as a routine quality measure.

items.headline: Opioid settlement spending put more than $340 million into housing in 2025, more than the naloxone strategy
items.summary: A KFF Health News analysis published November 12 found state and local governments reported spending or committing more than $340 million of opioid settlement money on housing in 2025, about 9% of roughly $3.7 billion and more than the core strategy that covers overdose-reversal drugs such as naloxone. Connecticut's $58.6 million voucher program had moved about 170 people into housing by mid-September, though researchers note most people who are homeless do not have an addiction. Clinicians and policy leaders should ask how housing programs connect to treatment, since the data cover only publicly reported spending.

items.headline: Alcohol drives older adults' acute care visits while cannabis dominates among adolescents, study finds
items.summary: A study in the American Journal of Psychiatry of 1.36 million people ages 16 to 64 with a substance-related ED or inpatient encounter found alcohol accounted for 19 to 26 percent of adolescent admissions and 73 to 76 percent among ages 55 to 64, while cannabis ran 70 to 78 percent in adolescents and 10 to 11 percent in older adults. Alcohol-related admissions rose significantly among ages 25 to 44, and cannabis-related admissions rose fastest among ages 19 to 24. The claims data run through 2023, but they suggest screening and treatment resources should differ by age.

items.headline: Review: U.S. opioid crisis now driven by fentanyl mixed with other drugs
items.summary: A Frontiers in Public Health review of 86 publications and government reports from 2010 to 2026 concluded the U.S. opioid crisis now runs on illicit fentanyl mixed with stimulants, sedatives and adulterants such as xylazine and nitazenes. The DEA reported xylazine in 30% of seized fentanyl powder in 2023, and a CDC analysis cited in the review found only 25.1% of U.S. adults who needed opioid use disorder treatment in 2022 received medication. Authors argue single-opioid responses no longer match how people are dying, which matters for clinicians treating mixed-drug overdoses.
